newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Currency woes occupy ASEAN, partners talks.
newsitem.headline: Currency woes occupy ASEAN, partners talks.

text.p: Southeast Asia on Monday took its battles with currency speculators to a forum that included countries whose citizens have been accused of wrecking the region's foreign exchange markets and economies.

Nearly a week after Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad unleashed a torrent of criticisms about "rogue speculators", "anarchists" and "international manipulators", whom he said were deliberately plotting to undermine Southeast Asian economies, the currency issue remains as heated as ever.
Mahathir raised the topic at the opening of the Association of South East Asian (ASEAN) 30th ministerial meetings on Wednesday.

ASEAN foreign ministers carried on the momentum, saying on Friday in their closing statement they were worried about what they termed "well coordinated efforts to destabilise ASEAN currencies for self serving purposes".
The message was repeated as the nine-member ASEAN went into meetings on Monday with their 10 "dialogue partners", key Western and Asian powers.
Among the partners are the European Union, which includes the world's biggest foreign exchange market in London, and the United States, of which financier George Soros is a citizen.
Soros's hedge funds have been singled out for criticism by Malaysia and Thailand, which say they have been behind currency problems. Soros has denied the allegations.

Speculative attacks in the past month have forced devaluations in Thailand and the Philippines, prompted costly intervention in Malaysia and sent central banks in Singapore and Indonesia central banks scrambling to defend their markets.
U.S. officials attending the week-long ASEAN meetings were peppered with questions about Soros's alleged activities.

Mahathir himself said the topic was discussed during his meeting with the partners and that some of them suggested the matter be raised at the 18-member Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Forum in Vancouver in November.
Statements from senior Western officials about the currency turmoil were cautious, while appearing to reject the allegations.
"The United States has been watching developments in Southeast Asian financial markets very closely," U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Monday.

Added Stuart Eizenstat, U.S. undersecretary for economic and business affairs to reporters: "Currency fluctuations historically, whether in the U.S., or Mexico or Europe or Asia, are caused by economic forces, not by one individual."
He added, "George Soros is an honourable man, he is a man who has done a lot of good in the world."

Jacques Poos, current president of the European Union, told a Monday news briefing: "This currency movement needs to be analysed. One cannot say it's one single cause or one single person responsible for it."

Other participants said they believed ASEAN's economies would withstand the currency battering despite gloomy prognostications from Mahathir that speculators had wrecked decades of development in the region.
"The Australian government has every confidence about the fundamental strength of ASEAN economies," said Foreign Minister Alexander Downer of Australia, one of ASEAN's key trading partners.
Still, Mahathir was not letting the matter rest. On Monday, he said his government may consider taking punitive actions against speculators.
The comment provided some temporary relief to the downtrodden ringgit, dealers said. It recouped to 2.6230/60 a dollar after dipping as low as 2.6508 earlier.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-206 2323)
